brief: Deutsche Bank's September chartbook frames the global yield rise as normalisation rather than stress. US 10 year yields are only slightly above their average since 1800, and with nominal GDP at 6.6 percent year on year the gap to 10 year yields is about 180 basis points, so DB calls 4.8 percent fair if nominal growth settles at 5.5 percent and about 5.3 percent if it settles at 6 percent, before fiscal concerns. On the Fed, trend inflation stuck near 3 percent, ISM services prices paid at a four year high, financial conditions near their loosest since 1990 and payrolls trending up in 2026 lead DB to argue last year's insurance cuts look ripe to be reversed. For the ECB, the energy shock pushed the real deposit rate negative again and DB economists expect a hike this week and another to 2.75 percent in December. Iran-driven inflation has lifted Democrat Senate odds, which track Brent. Q2 global earnings growth was the strongest non-pandemic reading on record, driven by an AI capex boom where the top five spenders outspend the other 495 combined. The yen sits near 40 year lows despite compressing rate gaps.
